title: SYSK Selects: How Filibusters Work
summary: SYSK Selects bonus rerun of the 2013 Stuff You Should Know episode on filibusters. Hosts open by explaining the Selects format, then cover the filibuster's history from ancient Rome (Cato the Younger) through the Senate's 1806 removal of the previous question motion, Wilson's 1917 cloture rule, the 1970s shift from two-thirds to three-fifths cloture and the "threatened filibuster," and Strom Thurmond's 24-hour-18-minute record. They discuss Wendy Davis's 2013 Texas filibuster and Ted Cruz's 2013 speech, which they call not a true filibuster, along with other delay tactics, reform proposals from 2010, the 2013 nuclear option on executive and judicial nominees, and their cynicism about partisan gridlock. The episode ends with a listener email from a homeless heroin addict in Santa Monica asking for detox resources, and the hosts' call for help.

segments.title: SYSK Selects introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the new Saturday SYSK Selects series, explain that they are replaying a past episode on filibusters tied to the then-current Supreme Court nomination and threatened Democratic filibuster, and begin the show.

segments.title: Wendy Davis and Ted Cruz filibusters
segments.summary: Hosts describe Wendy Davis's eleven-hour solo filibuster against Texas abortion-limiting bills, noting the Texas rule that speakers stay on topic. They describe Ted Cruz's 2013 twenty-one-hour speech against a continuing resolution, which they say was not a true filibuster because it was arranged with Harry Reid.

segments.title: Definition and origins of the filibuster
segments.summary: Hosts define the filibuster as a way to block or delay Senate action, say the name likely comes from a Dutch word for pirate, and trace the tactic to Cato the Younger in ancient Rome, when Senate business had to end by dusk.

segments.title: Previous question motion and early filibusters
segments.summary: Hosts explain that the Senate removed the previous question motion in 1806, which opened the door to unlimited debate, and that the House kept it, so the House cannot filibuster. They note the first filibuster came in 1837 and fewer than two dozen occurred before 1900.

segments.title: Cloture, civil rights and Strom Thurmond
segments.summary: Hosts cover Wilson's 1917 push for a cloture rule requiring two-thirds to end debate, its use by segregationists against civil rights bills, Strom Thurmond's 1957 twenty-four-hour-eighteen-minute speech, and the 1970s change to three-fifths cloture plus the rise of the threatened filibuster.

segments.title: Other delay tactics and filibuster abuse
segments.summary: Hosts describe other ways to stall Senate business, including reading many amendments in full, roll call votes, quorum calls, and anonymous holds. They cite counts of threatened filibusters in 2007 and 2008 and discuss whether partisanship has worsened.

segments.title: Reform proposals and the nuclear option
segments.summary: Hosts discuss 2010 reform proposals that failed, the Democrats' and Republicans' use of filibusters on nominees, the 2013 nuclear option that set a simple-majority rule for executive and judicial nominees, and the dispute over the D.C. Circuit. They close with comments on cynicism about politics, and move on to a listener email.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts read a listener email from TJ, a homeless heroin addict in Santa Monica seeking detox and rehab resources, and ask Southern California listeners to help. They close with contact information.
